prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an interesting and timely problem: how to adapt concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model features when the deployment distribution shifts and only unlabeled target data are available. The paper’s central claim is that concept-based pipelines are not automatically robust under shift, even when the underlying foundation model is relatively strong, and that one can recover both accuracy and more target-aligned concept explanations through a three-stage adaptation procedure. Overall, I found the problem well motivated, the empirical phenomenon plausible and important, and the proposed method reasonably intuitive. At the same time, I have substantial reservations about the methodological grounding, the fairness and interpretation of some experiments, and the extent to which the method truly preserves or improves interpretability rather than simply reparameterizing a linear classifier in a concept-like basis.

The main strengths are clear. First, the paper addresses a gap in the literature: test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models, especially in the modern setting where concepts are extracted from foundation-model embeddings rather than manually annotated. This is a worthwhile direction because many recent CBM papers emphasize interpretability at training time but say little about post-deployment behavior under shift. Second, the paper identifies a useful taxonomy of failure modes: non-robust concept extraction under low-level shift, non-robust concept-to-label mapping under concept-level shift, and incompleteness of the concept set. Even if the formalization is somewhat loose, this decomposition is helpful for thinking about where CBMs can fail. Third, the empirical results suggest that unadapted CBMs can indeed degrade sharply under shift, especially on Waterbirds and Metashift, and that adaptation can recover a large fraction of the lost performance. This is an important practical message. Fourth, the method is modular: adapting concept vectors, then the linear head, then adding residual concepts is a sensible design that maps onto the proposed failure modes.

That said, I think the paper currently overstates both its conceptual novelty and the strength of its evidence. At a high level, CONDA is a combination of fairly standard ingredients from source-free/test-time adaptation and CBM literature: pseudo-labeling from stronger teachers, class-conditional alignment via Mahalanobis distances, linear-head adaptation with regularization, and residual concept expansion. The novelty lies more in the packaging for CBMs than in a fundamentally new adaptation principle. That is acceptable for a conference paper if the empirical case is strong and the framing is precise, but here several aspects need tightening.

My biggest concern is the role of pseudo-labels and the comparison protocol. The method adapts the CBM using pseudo-labels obtained from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors on the same foundation-model features. In practice, this means the adaptation signal comes from non-interpretable predictors that are often stronger than the unadapted CBM itself. This raises two issues. First, it becomes difficult to disentangle whether CONDA is genuinely adapting concepts or simply distilling the predictions of a stronger black-box teacher into a concept-parameterized linear model. Second, the claim that CONDA “aligns the CBM performance with that of non-interpretable classification” is less surprising if those non-interpretable classifiers are directly supervising the adaptation. In other words, the method may be borrowing robustness from the teacher rather than discovering it through unlabeled target structure. This does not invalidate the approach, but it should be framed much more explicitly. I would strongly encourage the authors to add controls that isolate this effect: for example, compare against directly distilling the same pseudo-labels into a target-domain linear probe on FM features, or into a CBM with only head adaptation, and report teacher accuracy versus adapted student accuracy. Without such controls, it is hard to assess how much of the gain comes from the concept-specific machinery.

Relatedly, the source-free setting is somewhat softened by the assumption that source-domain class-conditional Gaussian statistics in concept space are available. These statistics are estimated from labeled source data and may be nontrivial to store or release, especially if the concept dimension is large and full covariance matrices are used. This is not unreasonable, but it should be treated as part of the source information budget. The paper currently emphasizes “without access to the source dataset,” which is true, but the method still relies on source-derived sufficient statistics and a source-trained linear probe for pseudo-labeling. A more careful discussion of what artifacts are assumed available at deployment would improve clarity and fairness.

The theoretical formalization in Section 2 is useful as intuition but not yet rigorous enough to support strong claims. The definitions of low-level and concept-level shift are essentially post hoc characterizations in terms of whether concept-score or prediction distributions change under a chosen concept map and classifier. This makes the taxonomy somewhat circular: a “concept-level shift” is defined as one that changes concept distributions but not prediction distributions for some idealized mapping, and then failure is defined as violating that property for the deployed model. Similarly, the completeness definition is existential over classifiers in the hypothesis class, but the paper does not connect this notion to identifiable conditions or measurable quantities. I do not think the paper needs full theory, but the current formalism risks sounding more principled than it is. It would be better presented as a conceptual framework rather than a formal characterization of shift types.

There are also some technical issues in the method description. The Mahalanobis-distance objective assumes class-conditional Gaussianity in concept space, but there is little justification that concept scores from modern CBMs satisfy this, especially across diverse datasets and concept construction methods. Since the method’s CSA stage depends critically on this assumption, I would like to see either empirical validation or ablations comparing diagonal versus full covariance, Gaussian versus simpler prototypes, or CSA versus alternative alignment losses. The paper mentions that CSA is especially useful for low-level shifts, but the evidence shown is qualitative and limited. More direct diagnostics would help, such as measuring how concept-score distributions move before and after CSA.

The residual concept bottleneck is also somewhat ambiguous from an interpretability standpoint. Once the method adds randomly initialized residual concept vectors and optimizes them directly for target accuracy, the resulting model is no longer constrained to use human-meaningful concepts unless the coherence regularizer is genuinely effective. The paper claims that some residual concepts correspond to feathers, wings, and beak on Waterbirds, but this appears anecdotal and based on automated annotation. That is suggestive, not conclusive. More broadly, the residual branch may simply learn arbitrary directions in feature space that improve classification. Since Eq. (5) shows the final predictor is just a linear map on FM features factored through an expanded concept matrix, the interpretability benefit depends entirely on whether the learned vectors are semantically coherent and stable. I would like to see stronger quantitative evidence here: concept purity, nearest-neighbor consistency, human evaluation of concept labels, overlap with known attributes, or comparison to unconstrained residual linear features. Otherwise, the paper’s interpretability claims feel under-supported.

The experimental section is promising but leaves several questions unanswered. The main table is broad and includes multiple datasets and CBM construction methods, which is good. However, the results are mixed in ways that deserve more scrutiny. On CIFAR100 and Camelyon17, CONDA sometimes hurts the strongest CBM baseline, especially the Yeh et al. model. On Waterbirds, CONDA improves CBMs substantially but still does not clearly surpass the zero-shot baseline, which is itself much stronger than some adapted CBMs. On Metashift, the gains are dramatic, but again the pseudo-label teacher is already very strong. The paper tends to emphasize positive cases while downplaying negative ones. A more balanced analysis of when adaptation helps or hurts would strengthen the paper.

I also found the source-domain rows in Table 1 confusing. Some “w/ CONDA” source entries are reported for ZS/LP but not for CBMs, and it is not obvious why adaptation on source would be meaningful or how it is performed. If the method is evaluated on source-distribution unlabeled data as a sanity check, that should be explained clearly. More generally, the evaluation protocol for online adaptation needs careful discussion because sequential adaptation on the test stream can be sensitive to batch order, class imbalance, and temporal leakage. The paper says batches are randomly split and processed online, but I would like to know how many random orders were tried, whether results are stable across orderings, and whether hyperparameters were tuned on target-like validation shifts. Test-time adaptation papers are often vulnerable to hidden target supervision through model selection, so transparency here is important.

Another concern is the fairness of the backbone choices. For CIFAR, the paper uses an adversarially fine-tuned robust CLIP variant, while for other datasets it uses standard CLIP or BioMedCLIP. This is reasonable if motivated by domain fit, but it complicates the narrative that the method is broadly applicable and that CBMs inherit FM robustness. In particular, some of the low-level shift robustness may come from the specially robust backbone rather than the adaptation method. The paper should separate backbone robustness from CBM adaptation more carefully, perhaps by reporting standard CLIP results on CIFAR as well, or by showing that the relative gains of CONDA persist across backbones.

The ablation story is directionally good but incomplete in the main paper. The claim that CSA is most useful for low-level shifts and LPA/RCB for concept-level shifts is plausible and interesting. However, the evidence appears to come from one CBM method and a relative-improvement plot. I would like to see absolute accuracies, variance bars, and results across at least two CBM constructions. It would also be useful to compare the staged optimization against joint optimization of all parameters, since the paper’s design hinges on the decomposition into failure modes. If staged optimization is not consistently better, the conceptual justification weakens.

There are a few places where the paper’s claims should be softened. The statement that concept-based predictions “should, in theory, become more invariant to inconsequential input changes” is too broad; CBMs do not automatically confer invariance unless the concept extractor itself is invariant and the concept set is sufficient. The paper later acknowledges this empirically, but the introduction still leans on a premise that is not generally true. Similarly, the claim of being the “first” TTA method for CBMs may be true in a narrow sense, but given adjacent work on concept-based OOD detection, residual CBMs, and source-free adaptation, it would be safer to phrase this more cautiously.

On the positive side, I do think the paper has the ingredients of a solid contribution if revised. The problem is important, the empirical phenomenon is real, and the method is practical. The paper is also generally well written and easy to follow, despite some notation-heavy sections. The figures are helpful, and the decomposition into CSA/LPA/RCB gives the method a clear structure.

For improvement, I would prioritize the following. First, add stronger baselines that control for the pseudo-label teacher: direct target-domain linear-probe adaptation on FM features using the same pseudo-labels; direct distillation into a linear classifier without concept constraints; and a CBM variant with only pseudo-label cross-entropy, no CSA/RCB. Second, quantify interpretability rather than relying mainly on qualitative examples. Third, clarify the deployment assumptions, especially access to source-derived Gaussian statistics and the source-trained linear probe. Fourth, provide more detail on hyperparameter tuning, batch-order sensitivity, and whether target-domain validation information was used. Fifth, analyze failure cases where CONDA hurts performance, especially on stronger CBMs. Sixth, better justify or ablate the Gaussian/Mahalanobis assumption in CSA.

My overall assessment is that this is a promising and relevant paper with a good empirical idea, but the current version does not yet fully substantiate its strongest claims about interpretability-preserving adaptation or concept-specific robustness. I would lean borderline positive if the venue values practical adaptation methods and emerging work on interpretable foundation-model pipelines, but borderline negative if the bar for methodological rigor and causal attribution of gains is high.

In summary: the paper tackles an important problem and presents a sensible adaptation framework with encouraging results, but it needs stronger baselines, clearer accounting of supervision and source information, and more rigorous evidence that the learned residual/adapted concepts remain meaningfully interpretable rather than merely serving as a convenient factorization of a target-adapted linear classifier.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. It argues that although FM-based CBMs can be accurate and interpretable on the source domain, they can fail badly under low-level and concept-level shifts. The proposed method, CONDA, adapts a deployed CBM using only unlabeled target data and no source samples through three stages: (1) concept-score alignment (CSA), which updates concept vectors to match source class-conditional concept-score statistics using pseudo-labels and Mahalanobis distances; (2) linear probing adaptation (LPA), which updates the concept-to-label linear layer using pseudo-label cross-entropy with elastic-net regularization; and (3) a residual concept bottleneck (RCB), which adds new concept vectors and a residual classifier to compensate for incomplete concept sets. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial target-domain gains over unadapted CBMs, often bringing performance closer to non-interpretable FM baselines. The paper also presents qualitative evidence that adapted concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: adapting interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines at test time under distribution shift, rather than only adapting black-box classifiers.
Clear decomposition of failure modes into non-robust concept bottlenecks, non-robust concept-to-label mappings, and incomplete concept sets, which motivates the three-part adaptation design.
Method is modular and practically appealing: it assumes a frozen foundation model and source-free unlabeled target adaptation, which is realistic for deployment settings.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple FM backbones, and multiple CBM construction methods, showing broad applicability.
Results demonstrate large improvements over unadapted CBMs on several benchmarks, especially under concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift.
The residual concept branch is a sensible mechanism for recovering missing concepts and preserving interpretability better than simply abandoning the bottleneck.
Qualitative interpretability analysis is aligned with the method’s goals and suggests that adaptation changes concept reliance in intuitively meaningful ways.
weaknesses: The theoretical formalization of shift types and completeness is largely definitional and does not yield guarantees, identifiability results, or principled conditions under which the proposed adaptation should succeed.

The method depends heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictions; if these are poor or biased under shift, all three adaptation stages may reinforce errors. This dependency is acknowledged but not deeply stress-tested in the main paper.
CSA assumes access to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics in concept space, which is a nontrivial artifact beyond the source model itself and weakens the claimed source-free setting.

The empirical comparison is mostly against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable FM baselines, but lacks strong generic TTA baselines applied to the equivalent linear predictor or to the full FM feature classifier, making it hard to isolate whether gains come from concept-specific design versus standard pseudo-label adaptation.

Some results are mixed or negative, including cases where CONDA underperforms the unadapted CBM (e.g., CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 for the Yeh et al. CBM, Waterbirds versus zero-shot baseline), suggesting instability or mismatch between components and shift types.
Interpretability claims are mostly qualitative; there is no rigorous quantitative metric showing that adapted or residual concepts are more faithful, stable, disentangled, or human-meaningful.
The online adaptation protocol may be order-sensitive, but robustness to batch ordering, batch size, and stream composition is not clearly established in the main text.
methodological_flaws: The shift taxonomy is scientifically weak as stated: low-level shift is defined by invariance of the concept-score distribution and concept-level shift by invariance of the prediction distribution. These are properties relative to a chosen concept map and classifier, not intrinsic properties of the data-generating shift. This makes the categorization somewhat circular and limits its explanatory value.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is problematic: it defines completeness by existence of a classifier whose prediction distributions match across domains, rather than by sufficiency of concepts for labels. Matching marginal prediction distributions is much weaker than preserving correct conditional label mappings and does not imply semantic completeness.

The CSA objective relies on pseudo-labels and source Gaussian class-conditionals in concept space, but there is no justification that minimizing log(D_intra/D_inter) with Mahalanobis distances yields alignment of target class-conditional distributions to source ones. The objective is heuristic rather than a principled estimator of any divergence claimed earlier.

The Gaussian assumption for class-conditional concept scores is strong and likely violated, especially for high-dimensional concept spaces and multimodal classes. No evidence is provided that this approximation is adequate, nor are alternatives compared in the main paper.

The Mahalanobis formulation appears numerically fragile because covariance inversion is required for each class; the paper does not explain regularization, shrinkage, or handling of singular/ill-conditioned covariances, which is especially concerning for many classes or limited source samples.

The pseudo-labeling scheme uses an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictions and selects the more confident one, but confidence calibration across these two predictors is not guaranteed to be comparable. This can systematically bias pseudo-label selection.

The claimed source-free adaptation setting is weakened by requiring stored source-domain statistics {mu_y, Sigma_y} for every class in concept space. This is additional source information beyond the trained CBM and may be substantial depending on m and L.

Equation references and notation contain inconsistencies that obscure the method. For example, the text in LPA refers to the target-domain CBM via Eqn. (3), but the actual target CBM definition is Eqn. (5); such issues reduce confidence in mathematical precision.

Empirical validity is limited by missing comparisons to standard TTA methods adapted to the same pseudo-labeling backbone or to the concept logits directly. Without these baselines, it is unclear whether CONDA’s gains are due to concept-aware adaptation or simply due to pseudo-label fine-tuning of a shallow classifier.

The interpretability analysis does not establish that residual concepts correspond to stable or causal concepts rather than merely useful directions for classification. Automatic annotation of learned vectors is suggestive but insufficient evidence of genuine interpretability.
